summary: What changed with Wolfram API/MCP access, and what (if anything) must be done to keep the current capability level
logs: Research in. Sending a skeptic to attack the cheapest-sounding recommendation.

final.bottom_line: Nothing you have is broken, and nothing is switching off on any date Wolfram has published — your Wolfram access was working this morning and the endpoints it calls are still live. The important correction is this: the GBP 4/month is not buying you a separate "API" alongside the bridge. The key in your .env and the key inside WolframLocalMCPBridge.app are byte-identical because they are one subscription, and that subscription is the only thing authorising the bridge, so cancelling would switch Wolfram off entirely rather than just save money. Wolfram's new free endpoint does run the same kernel, same licence class, same curated data and the same three tools — but it forgets everything between calls, and it kills any single calculation at about 30 seconds. So: add the free one alongside what you already have, prove it on your actual workload, and keep paying the GBP 4 while you do, because there is no documented way to buy the subscription back once it lapses.

what_the_user_must_do.step: Keep paying the GBP 4/month for now. Change nothing about the subscription, the key, or the bridge app.
what_the_user_must_do.why: The key in .env and the bridge's WOLFRAM_AUTH_KEY are the same credential, and it is a bearer token checked on Wolfram's servers. If the subscription lapses the bridge does not degrade — it starts returning error text instead of maths. Until a replacement is proven on your real work, this GBP 4 is what is holding the capability up.

what_the_user_must_do.step: Add the free endpoint as a SECOND, separately named MCP server, leaving the existing Wolfram entry completely untouched. For Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http wolfram-cloud https://agenttools.wolfram.com/mcp — for Claude Desktop, a new entry in claude_desktop_config.json with just a url field and no env block. I can do this for you; it needs no account, no password and no key.
what_the_user_must_do.why: Both servers coexist without conflict under different names. This gives you a working spare before you need one, and lets you compare the two on identical queries rather than guessing. It costs you three extra tool definitions in context during the comparison period — small, and temporary.

what_the_user_must_do.step: Run the same WolframContext query against both servers and compare the two outputs side by side. Look specifically for whether the free one returns TWO sections separated by a ====== marker, labelled Wolfram Alpha and Wolfram Language.
what_the_user_must_do.why: Reading the bridge binary showed its WolframContext fires two separate Wolfram endpoints concurrently and merges the results. If the free endpoint returns only one source, your documentation search quietly halves — no error, just less. This is the single most plausible hidden capability loss and it is directly testable. I can run this for you.

what_the_user_must_do.step: Time your real Wolfram verification calls over one bench round. Flag anything that takes more than about 25 seconds.
what_the_user_must_do.why: The free endpoint was measured returning HTTP 504 at roughly 30.7 seconds, three times, and raising timeConstraint does not help because the gateway cuts first. Your current path completed a 45-second call. Hard FullSimplify, large DSolve and high-precision NIntegrate can exceed 30 seconds. You need to know whether that ceiling touches your actual workload or is theoretical. I can run this for you.

what_the_user_must_do.step: Check whether any CDSFL verification defines something in one Wolfram call and uses it in a later one (a helper function, $Assumptions, a stored expression).
what_the_user_must_do.why: Your current bridge keeps session state; the free endpoint explicitly does not. For one-shot cross-checks against SymPy this is irrelevant. If anything in the pipeline does chain calls, that work would silently return well-formed but wrong answers on the free endpoint. I can audit this for you.

what_the_user_must_do.step: Add a guard that treats any Wolfram tool result beginning with [HTTP Error, [Timeout after, or [Error] as a FAILED verification rather than as evidence.
what_the_user_must_do.why: This matters right now, independently of any switch. The bridge's own code returns every failure — auth rejection, timeout, network fault — as a SUCCESSFUL tool result whose text is an error string. An unattended run would ingest '[HTTP Error 401]' as though it were a Wolfram answer. This project has already lost a convergence to exactly that class of defect (the NOT FALSIFIED substring bug). I can write this for you.

what_the_user_must_do.step: Copy /Applications/WolframLocalMCPBridge.app and, if you still have it, the installer package, to external storage.
what_the_user_must_do.why: The app has no auto-updater and its English documentation and support articles now 404 or redirect to the free product. If you ever needed to reinstall it, the download may no longer be obtainable. A copy costs nothing and changes nothing. I can do this for you.

what_the_user_must_do.step: Read the two notices yourself and note the exact product name each one uses, and any date.
what_the_user_must_do.why: I could not find either notice published anywhere. If one of them names 'Wolfram MCP Service' with a cutoff date, that changes the timeline materially — it is currently the only unknown that could impose a deadline. This is your email; only you can look.

what_the_user_must_do.step: Log in to account.wolfram.com yourself and look at the subscription page and the developer API-keys page. Do not paste anything back to me — just read what product name is on the subscription and what the renewal date is.
what_the_user_must_do.why: This settles what you are actually paying for, and whether Wolfram has posted any subscriber-facing notice that is not on the public pages. It involves your account and password, so it must be you, not me.

what_the_user_must_do.step: ONLY after a complete bench run has finished clean on the free endpoint, and only if you actively want the money back, consider cancelling. Not before.
what_the_user_must_do.why: Wolfram states it does not offer refunds, the subscribe URL now redirects to the free product page, the old service documentation returns 404, and there is no published way to repurchase. Given you have said you would rather pay than lose capability, the honest answer is that cancelling has poor odds and small upside.

what_the_user_must_not_do: Do not cancel the subscription now — including 'just to see if it still works'. Cancellation appears to be a one-way door: no refunds, no repurchase page, and the old product documentation is already gone.
Do not delete, move, rename or modify /Applications/WolframLocalMCPBridge.app. It cannot update itself and may not be re-downloadable.

Do not replace the existing Wolfram MCP server entry with the free one. Add a new entry alongside it under a different name. Replacing it means losing the working path the moment the new one misbehaves.
Do not paste your Wolfram key into any configuration for agenttools.wolfram.com. That endpoint takes no authentication, and supplying a credential to something that does not use it is pure downside.
Do not treat a Wolfram tool call that 'succeeded' as a verified result without checking the text. The bridge returns errors as successful results.

Do not point an unattended overnight bench run at the free endpoint until it has been exercised under load. Wolfram publishes no rate limit at all — only the words 'limited personal use' and 'small-scale and casual use' — and there is no account, no ticket and no appeal route behind an anonymous endpoint.

Do not buy Mathematica, Wolfram|One or a Wolfram Engine licence to get 'Wolfram Local MCP'. That is the only route to a genuinely local stateful kernel, and it costs orders of magnitude more than GBP 4/month to solve a problem you have not been shown to have.

Do not let the old context-window worry drive this. The bridge is itself an MCP server exposing the same three tools, so switching is a swap, not an addition. Only the deliberate side-by-side period costs anything, and it is three extra tool definitions.
final.money: The GBP 4/month is buying bearer-token access to Wolfram's hosted MCP service at services.wolfram.com/api/mcp — which is exactly and only what WolframLocalMCPBridge.app calls. It is not a second, separate "API" purchase sitting beside the bridge; the identical SHA-256 on the two key names is because there is one product. An archived copy of the old product page (Wayback, 2026-03-16) describes it as a single 5 USD monthly plan with no tiers or overages, which is consistent with your GBP 4. Concretely, over and above what the free endpoint gives you, it buys three things: persistent session state between calls (measured — a definition set in one call survived to a later call on your bridge and vanished on the free one), a longer per-call ceiling (measured at 45 seconds succeeding on yours versus a hard 504 at roughly 30.7 seconds on the free one), and possibly a richer WolframContext that merges two Wolfram sources rather than one (confirmed in the bridge binary, unconfirmed on the free endpoint). CAN IT BE DROPPED? Technically yes — the free endpoint runs the same kernel build, the same Professional licence class, on the same production fleet, with the same three tools and full curated data. But it should NOT be dropped yet, and quite possibly not at all. Wolfram publishes no repurchase path, no refunds, and no notice about what happens to existing subscribers. Set against a project funded from borrowed money where a lost experimental run costs far more than GBP 48/year, the subscription is currently functioning as cheap insurance rather than as waste. Note also that your codebase reads WOLFRAM_API_KEY nowhere — three textual mentions, all documentation or an env template, zero actual reads — so cancelling looks free from the code side. It is not: it kills the bridge, and it turns those three doc mentions into misleading instructions pointing at a product a third party could no longer buy.
final.capability_risk: Two measured losses if you moved to the free endpoint, and one that has not fired yet on your current one. FIRST, statelessness. The free kernel forgets definitions between calls — this is stated in its own tool description and confirmed by direct probe. The danger is not that it errors; it is that a chained verification returns a syntactically valid but wrong expression, which a verdict-reader can score as 'not falsified'. For a falsification pipeline that is the worst possible failure shape, and this project has been bitten by that exact class of bug before. SECOND, a ~30-second hard ceiling enforced by an HTTP gateway, undocumented anywhere, which arrives as a transport error rather than a Wolfram abort — so an automated runner is most likely to log it as flakiness and move on. THIRD, and this one applies to your CURRENT setup today: reading the bridge binary shows every failure path returns a normal successful MCP result whose text is an error string. If your subscription ever lapsed or the key were revoked, the tool would keep 'succeeding' and hand back '[HTTP Error 401]' to be ingested as evidence. The bridge is also frozen at 2026-02-17 with no updater, hardcoded to the paid endpoint with no way to repoint it, carrying its own five-month-old certificate trust store — so a certificate rotation or protocol bump on Wolfram's side would break it silently and permanently. Against all that, the reassuring part is real: the free kernel reports the same version, same Professional licence, same non-expiring licence date and a neighbouring machine on the same cloud fleet, and returned correct results across Integrate, DSolve, Series, 60-digit N, Sum, Solve, FullSimplify, ElementData, ChemicalData, IsotopeData, EntityValue, GeoDistance and FinancialData. The symbolic-maths cross-verification workload that CDSFL actually runs is not at risk on either path.
open_unknowns: Whether any usage limit exists on the free endpoint. Wolfram publishes no number anywhere — no requests per day, no quota, no throttle. Tellingly, the old PAID page carried a 'How is usage limited?' question and said usage was monitored to prevent abuse; that question was deleted rather than updated when the page became the free one. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: only running a full bench cycle through it and watching for throttling or blocks. Do not probe rate limits deliberately — that would itself be abuse.

Whether an automated multi-agent research pipeline counts as the 'limited personal use' and 'small-scale and casual use' the free endpoint is offered for. Not defined on any page. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: asking Wolfram directly, in writing, describing the workload. That is worth doing before leaning on the free endpoint for published results.

Whether the free endpoint's WolframContext returns both source streams or only one. Your bridge demonstrably merges WolframAlphaContext and WolframLanguageHints. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: one identical query run against both servers, diffed — about five minutes of work, and it is the cheapest high-value test on this list.

Whether Wolfram is formally retiring the paid MCP Service, and what happens to existing subscribers. No deprecation notice, no migration plan, no cutoff date exists on any page. The evidence is circumstantial but consistent: the subscribe URL 301-redirects to the free product, the service documentation 404s, the support article for your exact Bridge setup redirects to the free article, one support article is stuck in a redirect loop, and the current product hub lists only Local, Cloud and Enterprise with no MCP Service and no Bridge. What survives is the German-locale copies. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: the two notices you received, and a direct question to Wolfram support.

What your two notices actually say. I could not find either published anywhere, and could not match them to a specific announced change. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: you reading them and quoting the product name and any date.

Whether the subscription remains purchasable at all, and what your renewal date is. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: your own account page. This is the input that decides how much time you have to run the comparison unhurried.

The true per-call ceiling on your current paid path. It completed 45 seconds; a 110-second attempt hit the local MCP client's own timeout before the service's limit, so the honest statement is 'at least 45 seconds', not 'unlimited'. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: a bisect between 45 and 110 seconds with a raised client timeout.

Whether the free endpoint is served at lower priority or a smaller share of the fleet than paid traffic. Invisible from inside the kernel — both report the same hardware. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: only sustained comparative latency measurement under load.

Whether the ~30-second gateway cut is fixed policy or an incidental proxy setting. Consistent across three trials, documented nowhere, so it could move in either direction without notice. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: nothing published; re-measure periodically.

The terms-of-use position, which you should read yourself rather than take my reading of. The Wolfram Cloud terms — the URL the free endpoint advertises in its own response header — prohibit using the Services to train AI models, prohibit systematic extraction or caching, and state the Services should not be used in conjunction with your AI-powered tools or services unless a separate licensing agreement is in place. Wolfram also reserves the right to change, discontinue or deprecate any Service with or without notice. Those terms are not specific to the free tier, so this is not a change — but CDSFL is an AI pipeline that writes Wolfram outputs into a persistent evidence ledger intended for publication, and that is your call to make, not mine. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: a direct licensing question to Wolfram, which would also resolve the 'personal use' question above in the same email.

Whether a free Wolfram Engine for Developers licence qualifies for 'Wolfram Local MCP'. Wolfram's own page says 'Free with: Wolfram Engine'; another source insists a licensed Engine is required. Direct conflict, unresolved, and the documentation sub-page 404s. This is the only potential zero-cost route to a genuinely local, stateful, unlimited kernel, so it is worth resolving eventually — but not now, and not as part of this decision.

research.question: What exactly is the Wolfram MCP cloud offering at agenttools.wolfram.com/mcp, and what does using it require?
research.answer:
SHORT VERSION: It is free, needs no account, no sign-in and no API key, exposes exactly the same three tools the user already has, and is connected with a single command. Wolfram publishes no numeric usage limits at all — that is the one real gap, and it is a gap in Wolfram's documentation, not in my research.

1. IS IT GENUINELY FREE?
Yes, as far as every page states. Wolfram's own wording on the Cloud MCP page: "Free for limited personal use—get started for free immediately", followed by "or view other access options below". The MCP hub FAQ says "At this time, you do not need anything additional to use Wolfram Cloud MCP." The support answer is blunter: "Wolfram Cloud MCP is free to use and does not require any authentication."

What it is NOT described as, anywhere I read: a trial, a promotional period, a time-limited offer, or a free tier with a named paid upgrade path on the same endpoint. No expiry date, no "introductory", no credit-card-on-file language appears. INFERENCE (not stated): "At this time" in the hub FAQ is a deliberate hedge and is the only textual hint that terms could change. Treat the free status as current-and-unbounded-as-written, not as contractually guaranteed.

The "other access options" are separate products, not tiers of this endpoint: Wolfram Local MCP ("Included with Wolfram|One and Mathematica") and Wolfram Enterprise MCP (custom/site licensing, no public pricing). There is no advertised paid version of the cloud endpoint itself.

2. AUTHENTICATION
None. Primary source, support.wolfram.com/75237: "Wolfram Cloud MCP is free to use and does not require any authentication." Corroborated structurally by the setup guide itself — every published config block for the endpoint is a bare URL with no Authorization header, no token field, no env block, and no OAuth flow. No Wolfram ID, no existing subscription, no API key.

This matters for the user directly: their WOLFRAM_AUTH_KEY / WOLFRAM_API_KEY is not used by this endpoint and is not needed to connect to it.

3. USAGE LIMITS
UNKNOWN, and I want to be exact about this. No page I read states a single number — no requests per day, per minute or per month, no kernel seconds, no CPU or memory ceiling, no concurrency cap, no rate-limit response documented. I checked the product page, the hub page, the agent-facing markdown, the support answer, the enterprise page and Wolfram's own GitHub reference. Silent throughout.

What IS stated is qualitative, and these are the only constraints Wolfram publishes for the cloud offering (verbatim bullet pairs from the Cloud MCP page's comparison list):
  - "Does not support sessions" — "Only single requests allowed."
  - "Does not support external files" — "Does not support file upload or download."
  - "For small-scale and casual use" — "Remote answers only, no local interactions."
Plus the framing phrase "Free for limited personal use". The word "limited" is never quantified anywhere.

So: stateless one-shot evaluation, no file I/O, no persistent definitions between calls. Those are capability boundaries, not throttles. Whether an unpublished throttle exists is genuinely UNVERIFIED.

4. TOOLS EXPOSED — SAME THREE, CONFIRMED
wolfram.com/for-agents.md names the endpoint and lists exactly three tools with descriptions:
  - WolframLanguageEvaluator — "Execute Wolfram Language code. Use this as the default for all computation."
  - WolframAlpha — "Natural language queries. Use for direct factual lookups when no code expression is needed."
  - WolframContext — "Semantic search of Wolfram documentation."
That is an exact name-for-name match with the three tools the user currently has. Same names, same division of labour.

Caveat worth flagging: WriteNotebook and SubmitPaclet also appear in the setup guide, but only inside client config examples demonstrating how to allowlist or denylist tools — not in any statement of what the cloud server provides. The larger tool catalogue in the AgentTools README (ReadNotebook, WriteNotebook, TestReport, CodeInspector, BuildPaclet, SubmitPaclet and others) belongs to the LOCAL paclet server, not the cloud endpoint. I found no page asserting the cloud endpoint serves more than the three.

5. HOW TO CONNECT — exact published forms
Endpoint: https://agenttools.wolfram.com/mcp

Claude Code, one command (verbatim from the setup guide):
  claude mcp add --transport http wolfram https://agenttools.wolfram.com/mcp

Claude Code, .mcp.json equivalent:
  {"mcpServers": {"wolfram": {"type": "streamable-http", "url": "https://agenttools.wolfram.com/mcp"}}}

Claude Desktop:
  {"mcpServers": {"wolfram": {"url": "https://agenttools.wolfram.com/mcp"}}}
The support answer additionally describes the GUI route for Desktop as going through Customize/Connectors and adding Wolfram, and for Claude on the web, using the connector directory and clicking Connect. The Cloud MCP page links Claude Code and Claude (web) both to claude.com/connectors/wolfram.

Claude.ai custom connector: Name "Wolfram", URL https://agenttools.wolfram.com/mcp

Transport is streamable HTTP throughout. No npx, no mcp-remote wrapper, no local binary, no headers.

BEARING ON THE USER'S ACTUAL SITUATION (this is the part that answers the two vague notices)
Wolfram's own GitHub reference doc, AgentTools/AgentSkills/References/SetUpWolframMCPServer.md, documents a DIFFERENT remote endpoint: https://services.wolfram.com/api/mcp, reached with "streamable HTTP with bearer token authentication", where you "Visit wolfram.com/artificial-intelligence/mcp-service to subscribe" and "Find your API key at account.wolfram.com/developer-tools/api-keys". That is the paid Wolfram MCP Service — and it matches the user's roughly GBP 4/month subscription and their WOLFRAM_API_KEY precisely. It also serves the same three tools (WolframContext, WolframLanguageEvaluator, WolframAlpha).

Crucially, that same Wolfram document describes that paid remote evaluator as "stateless, meaning that you cannot reuse definitions from one call to the next", operating under "fixed memory and time constraints". INFERENCE: the user is therefore already on a stateless one-shot remote service, so the free endpoint's "Only single requests allowed" is not a downgrade from what they have — it is the same architecture. This also explains the Linux kernel on a macOS host noted in the established facts: the Local MCP Bridge is a local stdio shim proxying to Wolfram's hosted Linux kernel, not a kernel running on the Mac. A Wolfram support article indexed as "How can I access the Wolfram MCP Service using the Wolfram Local MCP Bridge on Linux?" confirms the bridge is a front end to the MCP Service.

STRONG SIGNAL, STATED AS INFERENCE: three separate legacy URLs for the paid service now resolve to Cloud MCP content instead. www.wolfram.com/artificial-intelligence/mcp-service/ (the subscribe page named in Wolfram's own GitHub doc) serves the Cloud MCP product page. support.wolfram.com/73194 serves the Cloud MCP connection answer. support.wolfram.com/73463 returns a redirect loop. Wolfram publishes NO migration notice, NO deprecation notice and NO statement about what happens to existing MCP Service subscribers — I looked for one specifically and it does not exist on any page I read. But the redirect pattern is consistent with the paid MCP Service being folded into the free Cloud MCP, which is exactly what the user's two notices ("API access had changed", "MCP access is now free") would describe.

BOTTOM LINE FOR CAPABILITY RETENTION: on the published evidence, switching to https://agenttools.wolfram.com/mcp preserves all three tools by name, preserves the stateless remote-evaluation model they already have, removes the credential entirely, and costs nothing. The unquantified "limited personal use" is the only real risk, and it is unquantified in Wolfram's documentation rather than unresearched.

sources.says: The Wolfram Cloud MCP product page. States "Free for limited personal use—get started for free immediately, or view other access options below." Its comparison list gives the only published constraints, verbatim: "Does not support sessions" / "Only single requests allowed."; "Does not support external files" / "Does not support file upload or download."; "For small-scale and casual use" / "Remote answers only, no local interactions." Characterises the offering as Remote/Cloud/One-shot stateless. Lists compatible clients including Claude Code and Claude (web), both linking to claude.com/connectors/wolfram. States no price, no numeric limit, no authentication requirement and no expiry or trial period. Contrasts with Wolfram Local MCP, which it says is "Included with Wolfram|One and Mathematica" and supports persistent sessions, local file access and notebooks.

Wolfram support answer titled "How can I connect Wolfram Cloud MCP to my AI application?". Gives the server URL as https://agenttools.wolfram.com/mcp and states plainly: "Wolfram Cloud MCP is free to use and does not require any authentication." Describes the service as enabling MCP-compatible AI applications to access Wolfram|Alpha, Wolfram Language and the Wolfram Knowledgebase. Provides per-client configuration including Claude on Desktop via Customize/Connectors, Claude on web via the connector directory, and bare-URL JSON blocks for Cline and Cursor containing no authorization header or token field. States no usage limits.

Wolfram's agent-facing markdown index. Gives the Wolfram Cloud MCP endpoint as https://agenttools.wolfram.com/mcp, described as "No local installation required. Best for most integrations." Names exactly three tools with descriptions: WolframLanguageEvaluator ("Execute Wolfram Language code. Use this as the default for all computation."), WolframAlpha ("Natural language queries. Use for direct factual lookups when no code expression is needed.") and WolframContext ("Semantic search of Wolfram documentation."). Points to the client setup guide at wolfram.com/artificial-intelligence/mcp-service/wolfram-mcp-cloud.md. Says nothing about authentication, pricing or usage limits.

The client setup guide. Endpoint https://agenttools.wolfram.com/mcp. Gives verbatim configs: Claude Code CLI "claude mcp add --transport http wolfram https://agenttools.wolfram.com/mcp"; Claude Code .mcp.json with "type": "streamable-http"; Claude Desktop with a bare "url" key; Claude.ai custom connector as Name "Wolfram" plus the URL. No config carries a token, header or env block. Names WolframAlpha, WolframLanguageEvaluator and WolframContext as server capabilities; WriteNotebook and SubmitPaclet appear only inside allowlist/denylist config examples, not as stated cloud server tools. Contains generic client advice about Bearer tokens and OAuth for servers that require them, but asserts no such requirement for this endpoint. States no rate limits or quotas.

The MCP hub page. Presents three offerings: Local MCP (local, session-based, "Included with Wolfram|One and Mathematica"), Cloud MCP (remote, one-shot stateless, small-scale and casual use) and Enterprise MCP (custom, site licensing, no public pricing). Its FAQ states "At this time, you do not need anything additional to use Wolfram Cloud MCP." and, for the local option, "For Wolfram Local MCP, you need at least a licensed Wolfram Engine, Wolfram|One or Mathematica. No additional subscriptions are required beyond that." Contains no deprecation, retirement or migration notice for any prior paid MCP or API offering.

Wolfram Research's own repository (primary, Wolfram-operated org). Documents a DIFFERENT hosted endpoint: "The remote server URL is: https://services.wolfram.com/api/mcp", using "streamable HTTP with bearer token authentication", with "Authorization: Bearer <YOUR_WOLFRAM_MCP_SERVICE_API_KEY>". Instructs "Visit wolfram.com/artificial-intelligence/mcp-service to subscribe" and "Find your API key at account.wolfram.com/developer-tools/api-keys." Serves the same three tools (WolframContext, WolframLanguageEvaluator, WolframAlpha). Describes the remote evaluator as "stateless, meaning that you cannot reuse definitions from one call to the next" under "fixed memory and time constraints", and recommends local installation for computation-heavy or iterative work. Does NOT mention agenttools.wolfram.com anywhere. File's commit history runs to 2026-07-21, so it is actively maintained rather than obviously abandoned.

This is the subscribe URL named in Wolfram's own GitHub doc for the paid MCP Service. It now serves the Wolfram Cloud MCP product page content, showing the "Free for limited personal use" language. It carries no notice of a change, no deprecation statement, no migration guidance and no paid subscription pricing. Evidence of the paid service page being replaced by the free one, but the page itself makes no such claim.

Indexed by search under the title "How can I access the Wolfram MCP Service using the Wolfram Local MCP Bridge on Linux?" — which independently confirms that the Local MCP Bridge is a front end to the remote hosted MCP Service rather than a local kernel. Fetching it now returns the Cloud MCP connection answer instead, including the agenttools URL and the no-authentication statement. Another legacy paid-service URL now resolving to free Cloud MCP content.

States "Wolfram Local MCP requires Wolfram|One, Mathematica or a licensed Wolfram Engine" and that no additional subscriptions are required beyond that. Lists capabilities the cloud endpoint lacks: persistent sessions, local file access, notebook read/write, test running and code inspection. Does not mention the Local MCP Bridge by name.

Enterprise MCP page. Offers Enterprise Local and Enterprise Cloud variants with local compute, data privacy and scalable infrastructure. Mentions site licensing and bulk discounts but publishes no pricing, no comparison against the free cloud offering, and no scale threshold at which the free service becomes insufficient.

Third-party MCP directory listing (SECONDARY, low confidence). Lists the endpoint as agenttools.wolfram.com and a release date of 2026-05-09, but claims an API key is required and that the service has "a free tier available... you may benefit from upgrading to a paid plan". This contradicts Wolfram's own support answer. The wording is generic directory boilerplate applied to remote servers, and the listing does not name any tools or limits, so I weight it low against Wolfram's explicit primary statement.

unverified: Any numeric usage limit for the free Cloud MCP — requests per minute/hour/day/month, kernel seconds, CPU or memory ceiling, concurrency cap, or payload size. No Wolfram page I read states any figure. The phrase "Free for limited personal use" is never quantified. This is a documentation gap, not a research gap.
What Wolfram does when a user exceeds "limited personal use" — throttle, queue, degrade, block, or invite an upgrade. No page describes an over-limit behaviour or error response.

Whether the free status is permanent or revocable. No expiry, trial window or promotional-period language appears anywhere; equally, no commitment to keep it free. The hub FAQ's hedge "At this time" is the only signal in either direction.

Whether the paid Wolfram MCP Service at services.wolfram.com/api/mcp is being retired, and what happens to existing subscribers and their API keys. Wolfram publishes NO migration notice, deprecation notice or subscriber guidance that I could find. The redirect pattern across three legacy URLs is suggestive but is my inference, not a Wolfram statement.
Whether the user's roughly GBP 4/month subscription will continue to be charged, and whether cancelling it would break the existing Local MCP Bridge. No source addresses billing.
Whether services.wolfram.com/api/mcp remains live and functional today. I did not test it — doing so would require handling the user's credential, which is out of scope.
Whether agenttools.wolfram.com/mcp enforces anything at the network level (IP-based throttling, geo restrictions, robots/UA filtering). Not documented; I did not probe the endpoint.

Whether the free endpoint's WolframContext is the full LLMKit-backed semantic search or the reduced form. research.question: What is WolframLocalMCPBridge, what licence/subscription does it require, what is WOLFRAM_AUTH_KEY, why does it report a Linux kernel on a macOS host, and is it affected by the move to a hosted MCP endpoint?
research.answer:
SHORT VERSION: the bridge is not a local Wolfram installation. It is a thin stdio shim whose only job is to attach a bearer token to calls against Wolfram's REMOTE hosted MCP service. The token is the ~£4/month subscription's API key. If the subscription lapses, the expectation is a hard stop, not a degradation. But the same three tools are now available from Wolfram's free unauthenticated endpoint, so the capability is very likely preservable at zero cost.

1) WHAT PRODUCT INSTALLS IT, AND WHAT IT REQUIRES

Wolfram's macOS support article (support.wolfram.com/de/52853) documents an application distributed as "Wolfram MCP Service", installed to /Applications, whose binary lives at Contents/Resources/bin/mcp_server, configured in the MCP client with env WOLFRAM_AUTH_KEY. That is structurally identical to the user's /Applications/WolframLocalMCPBridge.app/Contents/Resources/bin/mcp_server. The Linux article (support.wolfram.com/73194) shows the same shape at /opt/WolframMCPService/resources/mcp_server.

Wolfram states the Bridge exists for AI clients that "cannot communicate or authenticate with remote MCP servers" (support.wolfram.com/73194, per the indexed article text). It is an auth shim, not a compute product.

CRITICAL DISAMBIGUATION, and this is where it is easy to get burned: "Wolfram Local MCP Bridge" and "Wolfram Local MCP" are DIFFERENT PRODUCTS.
 - Wolfram Local MCP = a genuine local kernel MCP server (the AgentTools paclet), requires Wolfram|One, Mathematica or a licensed Wolfram Engine, stateful sessions, local file access, notebook editing. wolfram.com/artificial-intelligence/mcp/local/ says "Free with: Wolfram Engine, Wolfram|One, Mathematica" and "No additional subscriptions are required".
 - Wolfram Local MCP BRIDGE = the shim the user has. It needs NO Wolfram installation. It needs a Wolfram MCP Service subscription API key.
The user does not have Wolfram Local MCP. They have the Bridge.

2) WHAT WOLFRAM_AUTH_KEY IS

It is the Wolfram MCP Service subscription API key, obtained from account.wolfram.com/developer-tools/api-keys. Both the macOS and Linux support articles set WOLFRAM_AUTH_KEY to "<YOUR-WOLFRAM-API-KEY>" and point at that page. Wolfram's own AgentTools repo describes the same key being sent as an Authorization: Bearer header to https://services.wolfram.com/api/mcp, and says a subscription is required to obtain it.

So WOLFRAM_AUTH_KEY is NOT an activation key and NOT a Wolfram|Alpha AppID. INFERENCE from format (flagging it as inference): Wolfram activation keys are dash-grouped, and Wolfram|Alpha AppIDs carry a dash (XXXXXX-XXXXXXXXXX); a bare 10-character alphanumeric matches the developer API-key shape, not either of those. This is consistent with — and independently explains — the user's finding that WOLFRAM_API_KEY and WOLFRAM_AUTH_KEY are byte-identical. They are one credential because they ARE one credential: the subscription's developer API key, which the bridge consumes under a different variable name.

3) THE LINUX-KERNEL-ON-MACOS PUZZLE — SOLVED, AND IT IS THE DECISIVE FINDING

The bridge does not run a kernel. It forwards to Wolfram's hosted service, which runs on Wolfram's Linux infrastructure. That is why $Version reports "for Linux x86 (64-bit)" and $LicenseType reports "Professional" — those describe WOLFRAM'S server-side kernel entitlement, not anything on the user's Mac.

Supporting evidence, all Wolfram-primary: the article titles are literally "How can I access the Wolfram MCP SERVICE using the Wolfram Local MCP BRIDGE" (i.e. the bridge is the access method, the Service is the thing accessed); the bridge's stated purpose is authentication to remote servers; the key is a bearer token for a remote HTTPS endpoint; the bridge requires no Wolfram product installed locally.

I did not find a Wolfram sentence that literally reads "the bridge forwards requests to services.wolfram.com". So the proxy conclusion is an INFERENCE — but a well-supported one, and the observed Linux/Professional kernel is exactly what it predicts. I rate it high confidence.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE SUBSCRIPTION QUESTION: because the key is a bearer credential validated server-side, a lapsed subscription should produce an authentication failure at the remote endpoint. That means the bridge would STOP WORKING ENTIRELY — not degrade, not fall back to a reduced tier. There is no local kernel to fall back to. I could not find a Wolfram statement describing the lapse behaviour explicitly, so treat "hard stop" as a predicted failure mode rather than a documented one. It is the conservative assumption and it points the same way as caution.

CAVEAT I MUST FLAG: the extraction of the German macOS article rendered one clause as the bridge providing access "without connecting to remote servers", which would contradict everything above. I judge that a mistranslation or mis-paraphrase of the surrounding sentence (the English Linux article says the opposite), but I could not re-read the German page cleanly to settle it. Flagging rather than burying it.

4) IS THE BRIDGE DEPRECATED OR SUPERSEDED?

No Wolfram page I read says "deprecated". But three independent signals say demoted:
 (a) wolfram.com/artificial-intelligence/mcp-service/ — the URL the AgentTools docs still tell you to visit to SUBSCRIBE — now serves the Wolfram Cloud MCP page, i.e. the free product.
 (b) support.wolfram.com/73194, indexed under the Linux Bridge title, now serves the article "How can I connect Wolfram Cloud MCP to my AI application?" instead. The bridge article's body has been replaced at that ID.
 (c) The current product hub wolfram.com/artificial-intelligence/mcp/ lists exactly three products: Local, Cloud, Enterprise. There is no "Wolfram MCP Service" SKU and no Bridge listed at all.
Counter-evidence that it is not yet removed: the German-locale article de/52853 still serves full Bridge instructions, and the AgentTools repo still documents the authenticated services.wolfram.com/api/mcp endpoint with a subscription requirement.

Read: the paid Wolfram MCP Service (and its Bridge shim) has been quietly folded into the free Wolfram Cloud MCP, with docs migrating rather than a formal deprecation notice. That matches exactly the two vague notices the user received — "API access had changed" and "MCP access is now free".

5) CAPABILITY PARITY — CAN THEY STOP PAYING?

The free endpoint is https://agenttools.wolfram.com/mcp. Wolfram support (75237) states it "is free to use and does not require any authentication". Wolfram's AgentTools docs describe the remote service as exposing exactly three tools — WolframContext, WolframLanguageEvaluator, WolframAlpha — which is tool-for-tool what the user has today. Both the paid and free remote evaluators are described identically as stateless with fixed memory and time constraints, so the user is not losing session state they currently have (they never had it — the bridge is stateless too).

The one hedge worth taking seriously is wording, not features: Wolfram describes Cloud MCP as "Free for limited personal use", "For small-scale and casual use", and says "At this time, you do not need anything additional". The phrase "at this time" is Wolfram reserving the right to change terms. No numeric rate limit or quota is published anywhere I read.

Also worth noting against the user's original reason for choosing the API route: switching from the bridge to the hosted endpoint does NOT add an MCP server to their context budget. They are already loading an MCP server — the bridge IS one, exposing the same three tool definitions. The context cost is a wash.

6) THE ZERO-COST FULL-CAPABILITY PATH, AND ITS UNRESOLVED BLOCKER

If they ever want stateful sessions and local file/notebook access (which the bridge has never given them), that is Wolfram Local MCP, and it needs a Wolfram product. wolfram.com/artificial-intelligence/mcp/local/ says "Free with: Wolfram Engine, Wolfram|One, Mathematica". Wolfram Engine for Developers is free. If a free Engine licence qualifies, that is a full local kernel at zero cost. I COULD NOT SETTLE THIS: one search-derived synthesis asserted the free developer licence does NOT qualify and that a "licensed Wolfram Engine" is required, which conflicts with Wolfram's own "Free with: Wolfram Engine" wording. I could not read a primary sentence resolving it (the wolfram-mcp-local documentation sub-page 404'd on every fetch attempt). Do not act on either reading without checking. Separately, Wolfram's AgentTools README notes WolframAlphaContext requires an LLMKit subscription, so even the local route is not subscription-free for every tool.

research.question: What changed about Wolfram API access in 2026, and does it affect a user who never called the API directly?
research.answer:
SHORT ANSWER: I found no evidence of any Wolfram API being deprecated, shut down, or requiring migration in 2026. What I did find is purely ADDITIVE — Wolfram launched a new family of AI/agent APIs and a free MCP service alongside the existing Wolfram|Alpha APIs, which are all still listed as live. I found no cutoff date and no action item for an existing subscriber on any Wolfram-operated page I read. That negative is qualified: I could NOT read the single most important primary source (see UNVERIFIED).

1. WHAT CHANGED AND WHEN
- 2026-02-23 — Stephen Wolfram published "Making Wolfram Tech Available as a Foundation Tool for LLM Systems." It launched three NEW access routes: (a) a Wolfram MCP service, (b) an "Agent One API" positioned as a drop-in replacement for a conventional LLM API, (c) fine-grained "CAG Component APIs." Date confirmed via stephenwolfram.com publications index and blog.wolfram.com's February 2026 archive. The three routes are confirmed independently on wolfram.com/artificial-intelligence/foundation-tool/ (Wolfram-operated).
- 2026-06-16 — Mathematica / Wolfram Language 15 released. AI Access Basic became included free with active Mathematica and Wolfram|One subscriptions, and the AgentTools/MCP framework shipped as a built-in.
- MCP made free — support.wolfram.com/75237 states plainly that Wolfram Cloud MCP is free and requires no authentication, at https://agenttools.wolfram.com/mcp. The marketing page frames it as "Free for limited personal use" and for "small-scale and casual use." This matches the "MCP access is now free" notice the user received.

2. WHICH PRODUCT'S API
Several, and they now sit side by side rather than replacing each other. wolfram.com/apis/documentation/ lists TWO distinct families: the new CAG APIs (Agent One, Wolfram|Alpha Context, Wolfram|Alpha Results, Wolfram Language Computation, Wolfram Language Hints — access granted by emailing partner-program@wolfram.com) AND the legacy Wolfram|Alpha APIs (Full Results, LLM, Simple, Short Answers, Fast Query Recognizer, Summary Box, Instant Calculators, Spoken Results). The legacy family is still documented as current, still advertises "up to 2,000 non-commercial API calls per month" free, and its Terms of Use still say there are no fees for the standard API Client. INFERENCE (high confidence, from the coexistence on Wolfram's own index page): the 2026 change is an addition to the product line, not a migration of it.

3. IS ANY ACTION REQUIRED OF AN EXISTING PAYING SUBSCRIBER
Nothing I could find. Across seven Wolfram-operated pages read end to end (apis/documentation, foundation-tool, mcp, mcp/cloud, mcp/local, products.wolframalpha.com/api, api/termsofuse, llm-api/documentation, api/pricing, support 75237) there is not one deprecation banner, migration instruction, sunset date, or "act before" notice. INFERENCE, moderate confidence: the notices the user received were marketing announcements of new capability, not termination warnings.

4. DEPRECATION OR SHUTDOWN DATE
None found. UNKNOWN rather than proven absent — see UNVERIFIED.

5. THE ~GBP 4/MONTH SUBSCRIPTION
The only Wolfram product I found at that price in actual GBP is Wolfram|Alpha Pro billed annually: £54.00/year, which the page itself renders as £4.50/month (monthly billing is £9.99). Student pricing is identical (£54.00/£9.99). Confidence that £4/month means Wolfram|Alpha Pro on annual billing: MODERATE — it is the closest published figure and the only sub-£5 GBP price I located, but I could not read AI Access Pro's price (the page shows tiers without figures), so an AI Access Pro subscription cannot be excluded.
IMPORTANT CAVEAT, and this is the finding most likely to matter financially: nothing on the Wolfram|Alpha Pro pricing pages (consumer or student) mentions API access, API calls, or AppIDs at all. The API's free tier — 2,000 non-commercial calls/month — is obtained by registering an AppID on the developer portal and costs nothing. INFERENCE, moderate-to-high confidence: if the subscription was taken specifically "for API access," it may never have been necessary for that purpose. I did NOT find any Wolfram page stating that a Pro subscription grants or enlarges API access. A secondary source claimed subscriptions include "a complimentary set of Wolfram|Alpha API calls," but I could not confirm that on any Wolfram-operated page, so treat it as unconfirmed.

6. DOES ANY OF THIS AFFECT SOMEONE WHO NEVER CALLED THE API DIRECTLY
On the evidence: no. The 2026 changes are (a) new APIs requiring an opt-in partner request, and (b) a free, unauthenticated MCP endpoint. Neither removes anything. Since all the user's Wolfram usage goes through MCP tools and nothing in their code reads WOLFRAM_API_KEY, there is no API-side migration for them to perform.
CAPABILITY RISK WORTH FLAGGING (this is inference, not a page statement): the free Cloud MCP is described by Wolfram as stateless, one-shot, for "small-scale and casual use," with no session persistence and no local file access. The user's current bridge gives a persistent Professional-licensed kernel. Swapping to the free endpoint to save money would therefore be a capability DOWNGRADE on persistence and scale, even though both expose Wolfram|Alpha and Wolfram Language evaluation. No published rate limit or quota figure exists for the free endpoint — the documentation page that would carry it (mcp/cloud/wolfram-mcp-cloud/) returns HTTP 404.

research.answer:
SHORT ANSWER: Capability parity is essentially established, and it is stronger than published sources alone would support, because I probed the free endpoint directly. It is the same kernel on the same machine fleet. There are exactly two measurable regressions, both real but both narrow: the free kernel is STATELESS between calls, and a single call is killed by an HTTP gateway at roughly 30 seconds. Nothing else I tested differs. The user should NOT expect a capability loss in symbolic maths or curated data.

METHOD NOTE (important for how much weight to give this): questions 1-3 cannot be answered from Wolfram's published pages, which are marketing-grade and quantify nothing. So I additionally made read-only, unauthenticated JSON-RPC calls to the public endpoint (Wolfram's own troubleshooting doc suggests `curl https://agenttools.wolfram.com/mcp`; the docs state it needs no authentication). No file, config, account or credential was touched. Findings tagged PROBE below are my direct measurements, not statements by Wolfram.

1. FULL WOLFRAM LANGUAGE KERNEL — YES, NOT ALPHA-ONLY.
PROBE: tools/list on the free endpoint returns exactly three tools with exactly the same names the user has today: WolframContext, WolframLanguageEvaluator, WolframAlpha. The evaluator's own description reads "Evaluates Wolfram Language code for the user in a Wolfram Language kernel." Executed successfully on the free endpoint in one call: Integrate[Exp[-x^2] Sin[x]^2,{x,-Inf,Inf}] -> ((-1+E)Sqrt[Pi])/(2E); DSolve of y''+4y==Sin[3x] (full closed form with C[1],C[2]); Series of Log[1+x]/(1-x) to O[x^6]; N[Pi,60] to 60 significant digits; Sum[1/n^2,{n,1,Inf}] -> Pi^2/6; Solve of a quintic (5 roots); FullSimplify[Sqrt[2+Sqrt[3]]-(1+Sqrt[3])/Sqrt[2]] -> 0. That is precisely the CDSFL cross-verification workload against SymPy.

SAME BACKEND, NOT A CUT-DOWN ONE. PROBE, free endpoint: $Version "15.0.0 for Linux x86 (64-bit) (May 6, 2026)", $LicenseType "Professional", $SystemID "Linux-x86-64", $ProcessorCount 2, $SystemMemory 135044562944, $LicenseExpirationDate {Infinity,0,0,0,0,0}, $CloudEvaluation True, $MachineName "wolframcloud-prd-cmp-4j-12". The user's paid bridge, same session, returned: identical $Version, identical $LicenseType "Professional", $ProcessorCount 2, $SystemMemory 135044554752 (8 KB apart), same non-expiring licence, $CloudEvaluation True, $MachineName "wolframcloud-prd-cmp-4j-2". Same production compute fleet ("wolframcloud-prd-cmp-4j"), same kernel build, same licence class, same hardware spec. The free service is not a reduced kernel; it is a sibling node of the one they are paying for.

2. CAPS — ONE REAL, MEASURED, UNDOCUMENTED CAP.
PROBE: a single evaluation is terminated by an HTTP 504 Gateway Time-out at ~30.7 s wall clock. Pause[20] returned normally in 23.7 s. Pause[27] -> 504 at 30.6 s. Pause[45] -> 504 at 30.8 s. Pause[70] with timeConstraint explicitly set to 200 -> 504 at 30.7 s. Raising timeConstraint does NOT help — the gateway cuts first. Note the inconsistency: the tool schema advertises timeConstraint "default is 60 seconds", which the gateway cannot actually deliver. By contrast the user's current paid bridge completed Pause[45] with timeConstraint 200, returning {45.001165, "bridge_d45"}. I could not find the paid path's ceiling because the local MCP client itself timed out at Pause[110] (MCP error -32001), so the honest statement of the gap is ">=45 s today vs ~30 s on free", not "unlimited vs 30 s".
PRACTICAL IMPACT: most Integrate/Solve/FullSimplify verifications finish in well under 30 s, but hard FullSimplify, big DSolve and high-precision NIntegrate calls do sometimes exceed it. Mitigation: wrap long work in TimeConstrained and chunk it.
EXPRESSION SIZE: not tested, not published. UNKNOWN.
REQUEST-RATE CAP: nothing published anywhere. The only language on any Wolfram page is qualitative — "Free for limited personal use" and "For small-scale and casual use". Tellingly, the old paid page carried a "How is usage limited?" Q&A; the new free page dropped that Q&A entirely. I deliberately did NOT probe rate limits (that would be abuse). This is the single largest residual risk to a heavy automated experimental workload and it is UNVERIFIED.

3. CURATED DATA — NO RESTRICTION FOUND.
PROBE, all on the FREE endpoint, all returning real values: ElementData["Tungsten","MeltingPoint"] -> 3422 degC; ElementData["Fe","ElectronConfigurationString"]; ChemicalData["Caffeine","MolarMass"] -> 194.194 g/mol; IsotopeData["Carbon14","HalfLife"] -> 5700 yr; EntityValue[Entity["Country","UnitedKingdom"],"Population"] -> 68682962; EntityValue on a species Entity -> mass interval; GeoDistance between two city Entities -> 3453.7 miles; FinancialData["AAPL"] -> live quote. Entity, ElementData, ChemicalData, IsotopeData all work.
ONE EXCEPTION, AND IT IS NOT A TIER ISSUE: AstronomicalData fails with "AstronomicalData has been superseded... not supported in the Wolfram Cloud Platform". I ran the identical call on the user's PAID bridge and it fails identically with the same message. It is a Wolfram Cloud platform restriction that they already live with, not a free-tier degradation.
WolframContext (semantic doc search) on free returned 14,819 chars including the same top reference.wolfram.com documentation hits the paid bridge returned for the identical query (CheckTheResultsOfDSolve, DSolveWorkingWithDSolve, DSolveValue, DSolve). WolframAlpha on free returned a full curated result with unit conversions. No quality degradation visible.

4. FREE VS SUBSCRIBER DEGRADATION — NO PUBLISHED TIER TABLE FOR CLOUD MCP EXISTS.
Wolfram publishes a Local-vs-Cloud comparison, not a free-vs-paid Cloud comparison, because there is no longer a paid Cloud tier. The three published options are Cloud MCP (free), Local MCP (needs a licensed Wolfram Engine / Mathematica / Wolfram|One on your own machine), and Enterprise MCP (contact sales). The user has none of the desktop licences, so Local MCP is not open to them without buying a product far above GBP 4/month.
THE DECISIVE STRUCTURAL FINDING: the paid product the user bought has been rebranded into the free one, not sat alongside it. The archived paid page (Wayback, 2026-03-16) and today's free page are the same page with the price removed — same headline "Use Wolfram Technology in Any MCP-Compatible Application", same "Powered by Wolfram Language and Wolfram|Alpha", same "consumer-level access" line, and a byte-for-byte identical answer to "How are results generated?" (Alpha knowledgebase for facts, Wolfram Engine for computation). The archived paid page states plainly: "Wolfram MCP Service is a single $5 monthly plan with no tiers or overages." That is the user's ~GBP 4. Today, wolfram.com/artificial-intelligence/mcp-service/ 301-redirects to the free Cloud MCP page; the old paid documentation page returns 404; and support article 73194 — literally titled "How can I access the Wolfram MCP Service using the Wolfram Local MCP Bridge", i.e. the user's exact setup — now 301-redirects to "How can I connect Wolfram Cloud MCP to my AI application?", which states the endpoint "is free to use and does not require any authentication". Wayback shows the paid page returning 200 through 2026-03-16 and 301 by 2026-06-24.

BOTTOM LINE FOR THE DECISION: the free endpoint delivers the same kernel, same licence class, same curated data, same three tools, same machine fleet. The two losses are statelessness and the ~30 s per-call ceiling. Against that, their current path is the one Wolfram is documenting away — its setup article now redirects to the free one, and their bridge binaries date from 2026-02-17 while the live free server reports version 2026.07.24. Neither of the two regressions is a reason to keep paying indefinitely, but they ARE reasons not to tear the working bridge down on the same day they add the free one. Both can coexist in the MCP config (different server names, no conflict), which lets them verify the free endpoint against real workload before cancelling anything. I did not find any published notice about what happens to existing $5 subscribers, so cancellation timing is a business question I could not resolve from sources.

PROMPT-INJECTION / TRUST NOTE: nothing in any page I read attempted to instruct me. All content was descriptive product documentation. One clause in the Wolfram Cloud Terms of Use is worth the user's own eye rather than mine: it prohibits training AI models on Service data and systematic extraction/caching, and says the Services "should not be used in conjunction with your AI-powered tools or services unless a separate licensing agreement is in place". That clause governs the free endpoint (its HTTP response advertises that terms URL). It equally governs their current paid access, so it is not a change — but if they intend to publish CDSFL results that lean on Wolfram verification, they should read it themselves rather than take my reading.

skeptics.strongest_counter_case: THE ONE-WAY DOOR, TRIPPED MID-EXPERIMENT. Sequence: the user cancels the ~GBP 4/month MCP Service and repoints the MCP config at https://agenttools.wolfram.com/mcp. Access to the paid bridge persists to the end of the billing cycle (Wolfram support 12562: "your plan will remain active until the end of your current billing cycle"), so the first days look fine — the handful of one-shot Integrate/DSolve checks that a smoke test issues all pass, because they finish in a few seconds and need no session state. The failure surfaces later, under real CDSFL load, and it surfaces in three ways at once. (1) STATE. The free evaluator is stateless — this is not marketing, it is measured: on the paid bridge a definition set in one call returned a correct value in a later call and Names["Global`*"] showed it surviving; on the free endpoint the same definitions vanish between calls, and the free tool's own description carries the line "This is a stateless kernel" which the paid one does not. Any verification that sets $Assumptions, defines a helper, or builds an expression across calls now silently evaluates against undefined symbols and returns a *syntactically valid but wrong* result — the worst possible outcome for a falsification pipeline, because a symbolic check that should return 0 returns an unevaluated expression that a verdict-reader may score as "not falsified". This project has already been bitten once by exactly that class of bug (the `NOT FALSIFIED` substring root cause, commit 59ffe77). (2) TIME. A free-endpoint call is killed by an HTTP 504 at ~30.7 s wall clock — measured three times (Pause[27], Pause[45], Pause[70]) — and raising timeConstraint does not help, even though the tool schema advertises a 60 s default. The paid path completed Pause[45]. Hard FullSimplify, large DSolve and high-precision NIntegrate routinely exceed 30 s. The failure arrives as a transport-layer 504, not a Wolfram $Aborted, so it does not look like a computation result at all — it looks like a flaky tool, which an automated runner is most likely to retry, log, and move past. (3) VOLUME. A bench run cross-verifies many claims per round across many rounds, unattended, from one IP, with no account attached because the endpoint is unauthenticated. Wolfram publishes no rate limit — the only wording anywhere is "Free for limited personal use" and "For small-scale and casual use", and tellingly the *paid* page's "How is usage limited?" Q&A was deleted rather than carried over. An automated multi-agent research pipeline is not casual personal use by any reading. The Wolfram Cloud terms additionally state the Services "should not be used in conjunction with your AI-powered tools or services unless a separate licensing agreement is in place", prohibit scraping or bulk download, and prohibit using the Services to "cache, or otherwise store data in a manner that circumvents the intended usage" — which is an uncomfortable fit for a project that writes Wolfram verification outputs into a persistent evidence ledger. Against an anonymous IP, Wolfram's cheapest enforcement is a block, and there is no account, no ticket standing and no SLA to appeal with (terms: Wolfram does not warrant operation "error free or uninterrupted"). NOW THE DOOR. By the time any of this is visible, the subscription is gone and there is no documented way to buy it back: the subscribe URL named in Wolfram's own AgentTools docs (wolfram.com/artificial-intelligence/mcp-service/) 301-redirects to the free product page, the old service documentation 404s, support article 73194 — the article for this exact Local MCP Bridge setup — now redirects to the free Cloud MCP article, and Wolfram support 69174 states "Wolfram does not offer refunds." There is no paid tier of the free endpoint and no way to purchase capacity on it. evidence: DECISIVE, and it is the answer to the user's actual fear. I unpacked the bridge binary (PyInstaller archive, Python 3.13, read in memory, nothing written) at /Applications/WolframLocalMCPBridge.app/Contents/Resources/bin/mcp_server and disassembled tools/language_evaluator_tool.py. EVERY failure path returns a normal successful MCP tool result whose text is an error string — it never raises. Bytecode confirms three handlers: TimeoutException -> TextContent('[Timeout after ' ...) -> RETURN_VALUE; HTTPStatusError -> TextContent('[HTTP Error ' + status_code) -> RETURN_VALUE; bare Exception -> TextContent('[Error] ' ...) -> RETURN_VALUE. CONSEQUENCE: if the subscription lapses, the key is revoked, or Wolfram switches the endpoint off, the tool call SUCCEEDS at the protocol level and hands back the literal string '[HTTP Error 401]'. An unattended CDSFL run that treats a returned tool result as a completed verification will ingest that string as if it were a Wolfram answer. This is the exact 'discover mid-experiment' scenario, and it is worse than a crash, because a crash is visible. This is verified from the binary, not inferred.

DECISIVE #2: the bridge is hard-wired to the PAID endpoint with no fallback and no override. Disassembly shows PROXY_URL assigned by LOAD_CONST (a module constant, NOT os.getenv): 'https://services.wolfram.com/api/mcp/v1/WolframLanguageCompute'. The other two tools are likewise hardcoded to /v1/WolframAlphaResult, /v1/WolframAlphaContext and /v1/WolframLanguageHints. Only WOLFRAM_AUTH_KEY comes from getenv. There is no configuration, env var or flag anywhere in the binary that can point it at agenttools.wolfram.com. If services.wolfram.com/api/mcp/v1/* ever stops answering, the installed bridge has no degraded mode and no alternate route — it just starts returning '[HTTP Error nnn]' strings forever.

The bridge can never fix itself. Info.plist: CFBundleShortVersionString 1.0, CFBundleVersion 1, CFBundleIdentifier com.wolfram.WolframMCPService. codesign shows 'Developer ID Application: Wolfram Research, Inc (D2Y8ST33G6)', Timestamp 17 Feb 2026 18:15:49. The risk that is NOT low: Wolfram can change the 'name' field at will, and the user's tool identifiers (mcp__Wolfram__WolframLanguageEvaluator, etc.) are derived from it. ======

' separator, labelled 'Wolfram Alpha' and 'Wolfram Language'.
